title: Saying thank you to the thankless occupation
article: On Oct. 29, Ian Bush was shot in Houston, B.C. after allegedly becoming violent while in RCMP custody. Police had arrested him for possessing an open beer at a local hockey game and giving a false name to an officer as a joke. Approximately three years ago, Keyvan Tabesh was shot by police in Port Moody.
In both cases the suspicion was cast immediately on police. In fact, in almost every situation like these there is a public outcry against the police.

In Bush's case, the details are still obscure and an investigation must go forward. He did not have a criminal record and everyone who knows him states that such violent behaviour would be totally out of character for the young man. It may turn out that the officer in question responded with unnecessary force, but the investigation should go forward with the goal of finding the truth of what happened.

The Tabesh case has a different nature. Although his death was tragic and I sympathize fully with the family, Tabesh had already threatened one citizen in her car. He then charged a plainclothes officer with a machete. The officer responded by shooting Tabesh. There were allegations from some of the public and Tabesh's family that the officer did not identify himself properly.
There is a clause in Canadian law for self-defence. Even an ordinary citizen could claim this had they been in the officer's position, although they would have had to explain the gun.

In addition, Tabesh was shot only one metre away from the officer. I am six-foot-four-inches and I could easily hit a target one metre away with a weapon such as a machete; so could someone much smaller than me. That Tabesh had closed to this range tells me that he intended to strike the officer. Yet, despite all this, there is a lawsuit against the officer and there was a ripple of distrust throughout the public.
No, police officers are not angels that will never do wrong. Some will act foolishly and some will be corrupt. Those officers should be reprimanded, fired or prosecuted accordingly.

But there are many others who go to work every day, filling a thankless position that the citizenry does not even begin to fully appreciate. Police shootings and other incidents should be investigated; but while we treat all criminals as "innocent until proven guilty," we treat our police officers as guilty no matter the evidence or lack of such.
Why do we raise an outcry against police every time there is an incident, instead of waiting or searching for the truth?

Even in the infamous GM Place riot after the Guns and Roses cancellation, closer analysis of footage of an officer "cross- checking" a man with his nightstick revealed that the officer could have only had one hand on that nightstick. The media did not point this out until some time after the incident. While this is not to say that the officer in question acted appropriately, a man shows a mouthful of broken teeth and everyone assumes it was the police. He was in a riot. Riots are typically violent. It could have been another citizen or even another officer that hit the man, but the public saw a video clip and a picture and assumed they knew exactly what happened.

It is time that the public acknowledged what police officers do for us every day. It is time that the public starts trying to understand the events and motivations in so-called "police- incidents" rather than just decrying the behaviour of the involved officers without knowledge of the affair.
There is no national day to honour police and they are rarely thanked.
So for every officer that is out there enforcing the law in good conscience and keeping me safe, thank you.
